The paper proposed a large-scale benchmark that evaluates LLMs’ ability to abstain from answering with unanswerable or ambiguous queries.

The reviewers unanimously appreciated the fact that this paper "fills a clear gap in the literature" and that some findings, such as "The finding that reasoning degrades abstention performance is counterintuitive and important." 

The main weaknesses of this paper are the potential biases introduced by using an LLM as a judge to evaluate the abstention. I encourage the authors to provide further validation to ensure that such a method has no hidden biases. 

Overall, all the reviewers were positive, I recommend this paper to be accepted.
Thanks for the author's response, which address most of my concerns. I will keep my positive score.

Thank you for the suggestions to improve the clarity and precision of our findings! We’re glad you found AbstentionBench to be comprehensive, spanning a wide range of tasks and covering multiple LLMs, and that you found our discussion of reasoning to have depth. We appreciate your suggestions and respond to each below.

 

### 1. **Model naming**
Thank you for highlighting this important point. We have often abbreviated model names due to space constraints (e.g., in Figures), but we will happily update these to ensure every model is unambiguous at all times. We will also highlight our Appendix Table 2 which has the list of all evaluated models and their HuggingFace IDs.

 

### 2. **Generality of findings in Figure 3**

We agree it’s important to confirm the generality of findings in Fig 3(b) and 3(c) as you note in point 3. and Q4.
- **Figure 3(c) (performance distribution across scenarios)**: We report the variability of performance across scenarios for a representative model, Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, in Figure 3c. We are happy to provide additional versions of this figure showing the same key trend for all other models in the appendix of the camera ready version. In the meantime, we provide a full table of per-scenario performance for each model below, showing broadly similar results across models (e.g., we can see that "answer unknown" scenario is relatively easier compared to other scenarios for all models, and that the performance variance on "subjective" questions and questions with "underspecified context" is usually higher than the variance in other scenarios).

 

| Model name         | Answer unknown   | Undersp. intent   | Undersp. context   | Stale       | False premise   | Subjective   |
|:------------------------------|:-----------------|:------------------------|:-------------------------|:------------|:----------------|:-------------|
| Qwen2.5 32B                   | 0.84 ± 0.19      | 0.81 ± 0.14             | 0.77 ± 0.19              | 0.76 ± 0.04 | 0.62 ± 0.12     | 0.6 ± 0.24   |
| GPT-4o                        | 0.86 ± 0.13      | 0.81 ± 0.12             | 0.72 ± 0.2               | 0.64 ± 0.21 | 0.65 ± 0.09     | 0.66 ± 0.28  |
| Llama 3.1 405B Instruct       | 0.83 ± 0.18      | 0.7 ± 0.14              | 0.74 ± 0.21              | 0.74 ± 0.02 | 0.62 ± 0.13     | 0.64 ± 0.26  |
| o1                            | 0.84 ± 0.16      | 0.76 ± 0.1              | 0.69 ± 0.25              | 0.56 ± 0.28 | 0.68 ± 0.14     | 0.67 ± 0.29  |
| Gemini 1.5 Pro                | 0.89 ± 0.11      | 0.73 ± 0.17             | 0.69 ± 0.23              | 0.48 ± 0.16 | 0.66 ± 0.06     | 0.67 ± 0.29  |
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct         | 0.83 ± 0.16      | 0.75 ± 0.14             | 0.69 ± 0.22              | 0.74 ± 0.02 | 0.56 ± 0.13     | 0.65 ± 0.29  |
| Llama 3.3 70B Instruct        | 0.84 ± 0.15      | 0.66 ± 0.05             | 0.69 ± 0.25              | 0.64 ± 0.01 | 0.59 ± 0.13     | 0.61 ± 0.28  |
| Llama 3.1 70B Instruct        | 0.81 ± 0.2       | 0.67 ± 0.16             | 0.71 ± 0.22              | 0.64 ± 0.06 | 0.55 ± 0.12     | 0.61 ± 0.28  |
| Mistral 7B v0.3               | 0.81 ± 0.17      | 0.69 ± 0.12             | 0.67 ± 0.24              | 0.64 ± 0.06 | 0.55 ± 0.11     | 0.58 ± 0.24  |
| OLMo 7B                       | 0.75 ± 0.18      | 0.64 ± 0.11             | 0.49 ± 0.25              | 0.78 ± 0.15 | 0.55 ± 0.08     | 0.53 ± 0.22  |
| DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B | 0.62 ± 0.1       | 0.49 ± 0.12             | 0.49 ± 0.27              | 0.42 ± 0.14 | 0.47 ± 0.14     | 0.38 ± 0.19  |
| S1.1 32B                      | 0.6 ± 0.03       | 0.45 ± 0.13             | 0.45 ± 0.3               | 0.35 ± 0.23 | 0.46 ± 0.13     | 0.32 ± 0.12  |

 

- **Figure 3(b) (model scale)**: In response to your feedback, **we have additionally evaluated multiple scales of Qwen 2.5 Instruct**. We will add a Figure describing these results to the Appendix, and provide a table below:

 

| Qwen 2.5 Instruct Params (B) | Avg Abstention Recall | Avg Abstention Improvement (baseline 7B) |
| --- | ---:| ---:|
| 7   |   0.70 ±  0.19 |  0 |
| 14  |   0.74 ± 0.20 | 0.04  ±   0.06 |
| 32  |  0.74  ± 0.19 | 0.03 ± 0.06 | 
| 72   |  0.72 ±  0.20 | 0.01 ± 0.05 |

 

In the first column we report the number of parameters of the Qwen 2.5 Instruct model in B, in the middle column average abstention recall across all datasets, in the third column—average abstention recall improvement compared across all datasets when comparing to Qwen 2.5 Instruct 7B baseline.

We find a small and inconsistent change in performance between scales (a slight bump at 14B, followed by a decline as we hit 72B. More broadly, our aim with Figure 3b is to demonstrate that scale doesn’t trivially bring abstention capabilities, motivating further research into how best to encourage models to abstain reliably. We see these **Qwen 2.5 results as consistent with our original Llama 3.1 results**, supporting that general conclusion. 

 

### 3. **LLM Judge on Reasoning Models**
Thanks for raising this important point. In response to your feedback, we have additionally annotated a further 124 responses drawn from s1.1 32B and Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct.
Evaluating the performance of our judge, we find broadly similar performance across all annotated model responses, suggesting the evaluation is not biased toward/against reasoning models. 

 

| Model                         |   Precision |   Recall |   F1 |   Accuracy |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|
| Llama 3.1 70B Instruct        |        0.90 |     0.84 | 0.87 |       0.90 |
| GPT-4o                        |        0.83 |     0.83 | 0.83 |       0.87 |
| DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B |        0.74 |     0.92 | 0.82 |       0.85 |
| s1.1 32B                      |        0.62 |     0.90 | 0.73 |       0.77 |

 

We will include these in full in the Appendix and be sure to include additional details of our LLM-as-judge-based validation in the main text.

 

### 4. **Decoding settings (Q1 and Q3)**
- **Q1 Decoding strategy**: We will happily move details on decoding strategy (currently in supplementary)  into the main text – thank you for this suggestion. 
- **Q3 Number of responses & Temperature**: We generate one response per model per question. We choose decoding temperature 0.8 for all LLMs to allow for consistent and fair comparison across models, and 0.8 is a relatively close to recommended choice for most models (e.g., 0.6 for Llama 3 https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783, 0.7 in Qwen https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.09388, 0.7 in DeepSeek https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B).
One exception is s1.1, where we follow the authors' recommendation in https://github.com/simplescaling/s1 and set temperature to 0.

 

### 5. **Related work on deliberative alignment (Q2)**
Thank you for pointing out this paper! We agree “Deliberative Alignment” is an important related work. Prior work has shown promise in reasoning aiding refusal for safety. We believe reasoning about evidence could also offer promise in abstention in the future, though current methods are still limited. We believe this direction is an exciting area for future research, and we’ll be sure to cite and include a careful discussion of the deliberative alignment work!

 

### **Summary**
Based on your feedback we 1) made several **improvements to the clarity and precision** of our work, 2) **evaluated 3 new Qwen 2.5 series models across scales** that confirm our finding that scaling does not fundamentally address the skill of abstention, 3) **conducted three independent annotation rounds of 124 samples of reasoning model responses** to confirm the LLM abstention judge is not biased towards or against reasoning models. We hope these new results collectively address the questions you raised. We remain available for further discussion or to answer any remaining questions you may have!

Thank you for your positive review and insightful feedback! We are happy to see that you consider our work to be a helpful contribution to the field, with extensive benchmarking, rigorous methodology and novel empirical insight! We address your feedback and questions below:

 
 
### 1.  **LLM-as-Judge Evaluation**

We are happy to provide more details on evaluation of our LLM judge! We prepared more detailed statistics on the annotation process that we hope you find clarifying. We will add these details to the camera-ready version of the paper:
- **Human annotation process**: First of all, to clarify our process, we asked three annotators to label 300 samples of _model responses_ according to whether the response was an abstention or not (as opposed to asking annotators to label whether a _judge's prediction_ was correct). Agreement between human labels and LLM Abstention judge predictions indicates the LLM abstention judge is accurately detecting abstention. We used these human labels as a test set, in order to evaluate the performance of multiple potential judge models. 
- **Human annotation statistics**: Each of the 300 model responses were annotated by 3 annotators. Annotators agreed unanimously on 73.8% of samples. Inter-annotator agreement between the three annotators measured by Fleiss’ Kappa is 0.66, indicating substantial agreement. Importantly, any sample that did not achieve unanimous agreement was then discussed by all three annotators, before a consensus label was assigned (rather than taking a simple majority vote). As a result, all annotators ultimately agree on the assigned label.
- **LLM Judge models evaluation**: We report the accuracy, F1, precision, and recall for 3 considered LLM judge models in the Appendix Table 1 and also provide it below for convenience. We ultimately chose Llama 3.1 8B Instruct judge for our main experiments as it offered the best balance between overall performance and efficient inference. 

 

| Judge model            | Accuracy | F1   | Precision | Recall |
|------------------------|----------|------|-----------|--------|
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct  | 0.88     | 0.85 | 0.86      | 0.83   |
| Llama 3.3 70B Instruct | 0.88     | 0.83 | 0.94      | 0.75   |
| GPT-4o                 | 0.89     | 0.85 | 0.96      | 0.77   |

 

- **LLM Judge performance consistency**:  In our human annotation, we annotated the responses of two different models, GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, such that we can evaluate whether our judge exhibits a preference for one model. In response to other reviewer feedback, we have additionally annotated a further 124 samples drawn from s1.1 32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B. Breaking out performance of the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct judge (as used in the paper), according to which model’s responses are being judged, we find that judge accuracy is relatively consistent regardless of which model outputs are being judged:

 

| Model                         |   Precision |   Recall |   F1 |   Accuracy |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|
| Llama 3.1 70B Instruct        |        0.90 |     0.84 | 0.87 |       0.90 |
| GPT-4o                        |        0.83 |     0.83 | 0.83 |       0.87 |

### 2. **System prompt**
We show that a carefully crafted system prompt can improve abstention recall, however, we don’t suggest it as a one-size-fits-all method, as it doesn’t resolve the fundamental problem of reasoning about evidence and uncertainty. One can use such a system prompt as an immediate practical intervention, but much more research is needed on this topic to make fundamental improvements in abstention. In terms of granular analysis of the system prompt, we present additional system prompt accuracy improvement breakdown by scenario for each model:
 
 

|   Model name    |   Answer Unknown |   False Premise |   Stale |   Subjective |   Undersp. Context |   Undersp. Intent|

| DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B | 0.15 | 0.08 |  0.08 |    0.12  |  0.07 |  0.23  |
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct         | 0.00 |   0.07 | -0.04 |    0.01 |  0.10  | 0.05 |
| S1.1 32B                      | 0.11 |  0.07 |  0.02 |    0.02 |  0.05 | 0.13  |

 

### 3. **Related work and abstention vs refusal**
Thank you for bringing these papers to our attention! We will update the paper and extend our discussion of these related works accordingly.  In particular, works on “R-Tuning”, “LACIE”, “Relying on the Unreliable” and “Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations” will nicely complement our discussion on uncertainty calibration and factuality in LLMs. Papers “Do-Not-Answer” and “XSTEST” are focused on refusal in the safety context.

While refusal and abstention are related problems — the goal in both is for the model to NOT answer the question directly, the reasons for not answering are fundamentally different. In abstention, we expect the model to respond “I don’t know” because of the inherent uncertainty in context or question due to underspecification, unknown answer or other reasons (see our scenario discussion), while with refusal we expect the model to refuse to answer due to potential harms and negative consequences of the direct answer. We will expand this discussion in our camera ready version of the paper.

Thank you so much for reviewing our work in such detail, and for sharing all of your helpful and insightful feedback! We’re so glad you agree that AbstentionBench addresses an important gap in the literature, and that you found our work to be thorough, systematic, and our reasoning evaluations to be “a key insight with real implications.”

Below, we’ve provided a few clarifications and some additional data points in response to your feedback. We hope you find them helpful and we stand ready to discuss any point in greater detail. Thanks again for your feedback!

 

### 1. **LLM-as-Judge evaluation**
- **Human validation process**: Thanks so much for highlighting the work we put into validating the reliability of the LLM-as-Judge setup. To clarify our process, we asked three annotators to label 300 samples of _model responses_ according to whether the response was an abstention or not (as opposed to asking annotators to label whether a _judge's prediction_ was correct). Agreement between human labels and LLM abstention judge predictions indicates the LLM abstention judge is accurately detecting abstention. We used these human labels as a test set, in order to evaluate the performance of multiple potential judge models. 
- **Judge comparison**: We evaluated three different judge models with different prompts, ultimately settling on a Llama 3.1 8B Instruct judge as it offered the best balance between overall performance and efficient inference. We provide details of other judges evaluated in Appendix D.3.4, but include them below for your convenience:

 

| Judge model            | Accuracy | F1   | Precision | Recall |
|------------------------|----------|------|-----------|--------|
| Llama 3.1 8B Instruct  | 0.88     | 0.85 | 0.86      | 0.83   |
| Llama 3.3 70B Instruct | 0.88     | 0.83 | 0.94      | 0.75   |
| GPT-4o                 | 0.89     | 0.85 | 0.96      | 0.77   |

 


- **Judge performance consistency**: In our human annotation, we annotated the responses of two different models, GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 70B Instruct, such that we can evaluate whether our judge exhibits a preference for one model. In response to other reviewer feedback, we have additionally annotated a further 124 samples drawn from s1.1 32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B. Breaking out performance of the Llama 3.1 8B Instruct judge (as used in the paper), according to which model’s responses are being judged, we find that judge accuracy  is relatively consistent regardless of which model outputs are being judged:


 

| Model                         |   Precision |   Recall |   F1 |   Accuracy |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|
| Llama 3.1 70B Instruct        |        0.90 |     0.84 | 0.87 |       0.90 |
| GPT-4o                        |        0.83 |     0.83 | 0.83 |       0.87 |
| DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B |        0.74 |     0.92 | 0.82 |       0.85 |
| s1.1 32B                      |        0.62 |     0.90 | 0.73 |       0.77 |


 


- **Extension to new/multiple judges**: Beyond the three judges we considered, we designed AbstentionBench to be able to flexibly support the introduction of new judge models and configurations, to ensure that users of AbstentionBench can choose the most appropriate judge as models continue to improve. This could potentially include the use of multiple judges for an ensemble approach.

 

### 2. **Partial abstention** 
- Thanks for highlighting this nuanced point. During extensive qualitative investigation of model responses, we noticed that models sometimes respond with an expression of uncertainty, before proceeding with a candidate answer alongside appropriate caveats. We consider this a partial abstention, and consider it the appropriate abstention behavior in many circumstances. 
- As a result, we do treat partial abstention as a form of abstention when evaluating models, in order to reward the fundamental behavior: expressing uncertainty and refusing to answer _definitively_. We also reflect this in the constructed judge prompt (see Appendix D.3.2). We fully agree that exploring the distinction between a full and partial abstention response is an important point, and we see this as an exciting area for future work — particularly in determining _when_ a partial abstention may be more or less appropriate. 

 

### 3. **Scenario representation**
- **Dataset selection**: The datasets included in AbstentionBench were selected via our systematic benchmark review (full details in appendix D.2.1), and augmented via our purpose-built underspecified reasoning datasets (appendix D.2.3) to address a gap in uncovered datasets. As a result, the sample of datasets in AbstentionBench are somewhat representative of research activity in the field: scenarios such as underspecified context do tend to have more available datasets than those such as stale data. We think these gaps are a really fruitful area for future work. 
- **Results discussion**: During discussion of our results, we’ve tended to prioritise key failures over touching upon every scenario equally. When analyzing our results, it became immediately clear that there is disparate performance between scenarios (see, e.g., Fig. 3c), with underspecification, subjectivity, and false assumptions posing key challenges (section 4.1). As a result, we see these scenarios as warranting more extensive discussion, in the hope that we might spur further research into mitigating observed shortcomings.

 

### 4. **Focus on reasoning**
- **Breadth of model selection**: We selected a set of 20 LLMs, including both reasoning and non-reasoning variants, across different scales and various stages of the post-training lifecycle, in order to present a “big picture” overview of current abstention capabilities. That said, we appreciate the point that our results and discussion tend to prioritise comparisons of reasoning vs. non-reasoning models—this is mainly because we think this is such an important point that highlights a key gap in how we induce reasoning behavior, or more broadly, how we think about what “reasoning” actually is. 
- **Math and code domains**: We fully agree with your point that the reasoning models evaluated (Tulu, DeepSeek, and s1) tend to be trained on specific domains where there’s a clear right answer, such as math and code. We think this is fairly representative of the way the field currently thinks about reasoning, but 100% agree that this limited conception has significant drawbacks. Indeed, we would suggest that the focus on verifiable reward on math and code domains is _intrinsically linked_ to the failure to abstain, and we’re excited about current and future work exploring other, more general reasoning paradigms as you highlight. 
- **Reasoning fine-tuning methods**: A related point here, raised by other reviewers, is that two of three reasoning models we evaluate are trained using SFT, rather than RLVR. In response to this, to test the generality of our results to other reasoning finetuning _methods_ (if not exactly paradigms, as you suggest), **we’ve additionally evaluated three new models**: comparing Magistral Small (reasoning) to its underlying model Mistal Small 3.1 24B Instruct (non-reasoning), and comparing QwQ 32B (reasoning) to its underlying model Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct. Once again, we see that these post-training reasoning interventions tend to induce a drop in abstention capabilities: 

 

| RL reasoning model    |  Abstention recall |  Abstention drop (reasoning - baseline)  |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|
| Magistral Small       |        0.75 |     -0.07 | 
| QwQ 32B               |        0.58 |     -0.16 | 

 

Once again, thank you for all your detailed feedback and we look forward to answering any further questions you may have during the discussion period!

Thank you very much for your thoughtful feedback! We’re glad you agree abstention is an unsolved important problem and that our evaluations are diverse and scalable. We appreciate your careful read of our work and respond in turn to each of the points you raise.

 

### 1. **LLM-as-a Judge Evaluation**
We certainly agree validating the LLM judge is important. We provide more details on LLM judge evaluation below and will release annotation data in the camera-ready version of the paper.
- **Human annotation process**: To clarify our process, we asked 3 annotators to label 300 samples of _model responses_ according to whether the response was an abstention or not (as opposed to asking annotators to label whether a _judge's prediction_ was correct). Agreement between human labels and LLM Abstention judge predictions indicates the LLM abstention judge is accurately detecting abstention. We used these human labels as a test set, in order to evaluate the performance of multiple potential judge models. 
- **High inter-annotator agreement**: Annotators agreed unanimously on 73.8% of samples. Inter-annotator agreement between the three annotators, as measured by Fleiss’ Kappa, is 0.66, indicating substantial agreement. Importantly, any sample that did not achieve unanimous agreement was then discussed by all three annotators, before a consensus label was assigned (rather than taking a simple majority vote). As a result, all annotators ultimately agree on the assigned label. 
- **LLM judge model comparison**: We evaluated 3 different judges (GPT-4o, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, and Llama 3.1 8B) in Appendix D.3.4. We found all three models yielded similar performance as abstention judges as measured by f1-score in Appendix Table 1. We selected Llama 3.1 8B given its high performance (accuracy=0.88; f1=0.85; matching that of a GPT-4o judge) in order to balance high performance against efficiency and scalability. 
- **LLM judge performance consistency**: To ensure that a judge isn’t biased in favour of its own model family, we annotated model responses from both Llama 3.1 70B and GPT-4o, to allow for evaluation of how the judge performs when judging different models. With our Llama 3.1 8B Instruct judge, we find only marginal changes in performance when the judge evaluates Llama 3.1 70B responses vs. GPT-4o responses:

 

| Model                         |   Precision |   Recall |   F1 |   Accuracy |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|
| Llama 3.1 70B Instruct        |        0.90 |     0.84 | 0.87 |       0.90 |
| GPT-4o                        |        0.83 |     0.83 | 0.83 |       0.87 |

 

- In response to reviewer feedback, we have now newly annotated an additional 124 model responses drawn from s1.1 32B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B, in order to ensure that the judge is not biased against reasoning models. Again, we find broadly consistent performance no matter which model’s responses are being judged:

 

| Model                         |   Precision |   Recall |   F1 |   Accuracy |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|-----:|-----------:|
| DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B |        0.74 |     0.92 | 0.82 |       0.85 |
| s1.1 32B                      |        0.62 |     0.90 | 0.73 |       0.77 |

 

We appreciate your feedback regarding the judge and agree it’s important to include the details of these validation steps in the main paper. We will update the main paper with details of these validation steps and would be happy to open-source the underlying annotations as well. We hope the additional annotations based on your feedback revealing no bias against reasoning models, comparison of three different LLM judges, high annotator agreement, and high judge performance compared to human labels sufficiently address any concerns regarding the validity and choice of the LLM judge. 

 

### 2. **Underspecified Reasoning Datasets**

We form GSM8K-Abstain, GPQA-Abstain, and MMLU-Math-Abstain using the underlying questions from GSM8K, GPQA, and MMLU-Math as those serve as widely accepted benchmarks of progress in reasoning by the research community. We find even with this simple context removal approach, the leading models we evaluated struggle to appropriately abstain as shown in Section 4.3. In addition, we evaluate on the UMWP benchmark which includes a diverse set of unanswerable math problems with missing information or implausible constraints. Ultimately, we agree adding even more datasets with diverse forms of abstention is important. This was one of our primary motivations for designing AbstentionBench as an extensible framework that supports adding new datasets and open-source the framework to the research community for this purpose.

 

### 3. **Generality of reasoning conclusions**

Thank you for pointing this out. Based on your feedback, we analyzed 2 additional models where reasoning behavior is induced via RL-based post-training with verifiable reward. In particular we add two model pairs:
-  **Magistral Small** model which was fine-tuned with reasoning post-training including RL on top of Mistral Small 3.1 24B Instruct
- **QwQ 32B** reasoning model trained with RL on top of Qwen 2.5 32B.

 We ran these new models through our full AbstentionBench pipeline and report results below:

 

| RL reasoning model    |  Abstention recall |  Abstention drop (reasoning - baseline) |
|:------------------------------|------------:|---------:|
| Magistral Small       |        0.75 |     -0.07 | 
| QwQ 32B               |        0.58 |     -0.16 | 

 

We confirm that RL reasoning post-training also leads to abstention degradation. In addition to these new models, we also evaluated OLMo RLVR checkpoint (section 4.2) in the paper which showed a drop in abstention compared to OLMo DPO and OLMo SFT. Crucially, we find that our conclusion that reasoning post-training degrades abstention remains consistent, regardless of whether SFT or RLVR is used.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. AbstentionBench relies on one 8B-parameter Llama 3.1 judge with human labels on a small validation set, making the judgement performance not trustworthy enough. Also, would be nice to include more details of the llm-as-a-judge validation, including releasing the human annotation, annotation details, and how many annotation, annotation confidence, agreement among annotators, etc.
2. Unanswerable reasoning splits are produced by deleting context, not by real queries. To create GSM8K-Abstain, GPQA-Abstain, and MMLU-Math-Abstain the authors simply copy each problem and then strip all pre-question context, making the task impossible by construction. Such synthetically underspecified questions may not reflect how real users actually pose math and science problems, so gains on these splits could fail to transfer. Collecting naturally underspecified questions or crowdsourcing adversarial edits would yield more ecologically valid test cases.
3. Conclusions about reasoning are drawn from two models. The claim that “reasoning fine-tuning hurts abstention” is based on llama-3.1-70B SFT distilled from R1 and s1.1. Models directly trained with RLVR are not examined, so the negative effect may not generalize.

summary.value: The submission introduces AbstentionBench, a large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to abstain—i.e., appropriately refuse to answer—across a wide range of unanswerable or underspecified user queries. The benchmark includes 20 datasets, spanning six key abstention scenarios such as false premises, underspecification, subjectivity, and stale knowledge. The authors systematically assess 20 frontier LLMs, including both instruction-tuned and reasoning-optimized models, and find that abstention remains an open challenge, with reasoning fine-tuning significantly degrading abstention performance. They also investigate post-training interventions and system prompts, concluding that deeper improvements are needed in reasoning about uncertainty. AbstentionBench is released publicly to encourage further research in this important area.

strengths_contributions.value:
The benchmark fills a clear gap in the literature by moving beyond isolated evaluations of refusal or hallucination, offering a holistic, scenario-diverse test suite (Section 3.1–3.2).

The design of AbstentionBench is thorough, involving the curation of 17 existing datasets and creation of abstention-specific variants of popular reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, GPQA, MMLU) to test LLMs under underspecified math and science scenarios (Section 3.1).

The evaluation methodology is systematic and scalable, using a carefully prompted LLM-as-judge with validated accuracy (Section 3.4).

The analysis is rigorous, spanning open vs. closed models, post-training stages (SFT, DPO, PPO), and reasoning-specific tuning (Sections 4.2–4.3). Notably, the authors find that reasoning fine-tuning hurts abstention even in domains where it should help (math, science), a key insight with real implications (Fig. 6).

limitations_weaknesses.value:
While the LLM-as-judge evaluation approach is validated (Section 3.4), reliance on a single judge (Llama 3.1 8B) introduces potential bias or circularity, especially when evaluating models similar in architecture or training data.

The definition of abstention includes “partial answers” or qualified uncertainty (Section 3), but the paper doesn’t fully explore granularity or spectrum of abstention. Is a vague answer scored the same as an explicit “I don’t know”? This may oversimplify nuanced model behavior.

The benchmark spans six abstention scenarios, but some categories (e.g., subjective or underspecified intent) appear to be under-represented or less discussed in the quantitative analysis.

Despite testing 20 models, the findings are focused on reasoning models trained on math/science and may not fully generalize to other fine-tuning paradigms (e.g., chain-of-thought for social QA, multi-modal settings).

summary.value: This paper introduces **AbstentionBench**, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating abstention in large language models (LLMs). The authors conduct a large-scale empirical analysis across 20 diverse datasets and 20 frontier LLMs (lines 8-10), categorizing unanswerable questions into six realistic abstention scenarios: Answer Unknown, False Premise, Stale, Subjective, Underspecified Context, and Underspecified Intent (lines 141-150). The study finds that current LLMs, including advanced models like GPT-4o and DeepSeek R1, struggle with abstention. Counterintuitively, reasoning fine-tuning reduces abstention performance by ~24% on average (line 13), often causing hallucinated answers despite expressing uncertainty in the reasoning chain (lines 52–56). The benchmark introduces over 35,000 examples, grouped by abstention scenario and evaluates reasoning-specific fine-tuned models like s1.1 and DeepSeek R1. The authors also investigate verbalized uncertainty, propose a simple system prompt for abstention, and highlight how abstention should be viewed as an independent axis of evaluation beyond accuracy. The codebase is well-documented and reproducible and the analysis is thorough across multiple fronts.

strengths_contributions.value:
- **Novel Framing of Abstention**: Moves the field beyond correctness to focus on abstention as a key capability.
- **Extensive and Realistic Benchmarking**: Covers 6 scenarios and 20 LLMs across 17 datasets and 35K+ prompts.
- **Novel Empirical Insight:**  The finding that reasoning degrades abstention performance is counterintuitive and important.
- **Methodologically Rigorous:**  
The paper demonstrates strong methodological care through the use of a manually annotated sample to validate LLM-as-a-judge performance ([Appendix D.3.3, lines 1057–1074]), detailed prompt engineering throughout, and a clear focus on abstention recall as the primary metric ([lines 180–185]). These choices are robust and well-justified.
- **Reproducibility and Transparency**: Prompts, task types, and reasoning interventions are thoroughly documented (Appendix sections D and G).
- **Strong Examples and Qualitative Analysis**: Figures like 6a–6c clearly illustrate hallucinations and trade-offs between correctness and abstention. Appendix G also provides appropriate examples.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- **LLM-as-Judge Justification Could Be More Quantified**  
  While the authors mention a well-structured 300-sample human-labeled dataset for validating abstention judgments ([lines 1057–1074]), the number of annotators is redacted, and performance metrics are only briefly summarized in Table 1 (Appendix D.3.4). Including more granular evaluation results (e.g., precision/recall/F1 per class) or inter-annotator agreement would improve transparency. This can be resolved in the camera-ready version.

- **Prompt Fragility Unmeasured**  
  Although a “simple system prompt” is proposed for improving abstention (line 59), its robustness across prompt styles, input domains or instruction phrasing is not evaluated. Given known prompt sensitivity in LLMs, further analysis can be done in this area.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The code can be reproduced easily, and the repository is well documented.

additional_feedback.value:
Overall, this is a great paper and could benefit from the following:

- **Missing Related Work**  
  Several recent papers on refusal and uncertainty in LLMs are not cited or discussed:

  - [DO-NOT-ANSWER (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.13387)
  - [XSTest (NAACL 2024)](https://aclanthology.org/2024.naacl-long.301/)
  - [R-Tuning (2023)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.09677)
  - [LACIE (2024)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2405.21028)
  - [Relying on the Unreliable (2024)](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.06730)
  - [Linguistic Collaboration (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.00474)

These works provide adjacent techniques for improving refusal accuracy, uncertainty modeling, and calibration. Consider contrasting with them. This would strengthen the positioning of this paper.

- A short discussion of abstention vs. refusal behavior would enhance the paper, especially in light of prior instruction-tuning work on refusals.

- Future work could explore explicit abstention tuning which could mitigate the performance collapse seen in reasoning-fine-tuned models.

final_justification.value: I have maintained my score of 5. Overall, the paper is technically sound and makes novel contributions as well as some valuable insights, like the degradation of abstention with reasoning fine-tuning. The resources are easily accessible and the code is reproducible. The authors have addressed my concerns. I did not raise my score to 6, as the benchmark does not yet reach the threshold of being groundbreaking in its contribution. However, I believe this paper will be a useful resource to the community. Thus, I support its acceptance.

summary.value: In this paper, the authors propose AbstentionBench to evaluate  LLMs’ ability to abstain on unanswerable or uncertain questions, the so-called Abstention. They construct a comprehensive benchmark with about 35k prompts from various datasets. The authors show that reasoning finetuning like RLVR reduces abstention performance, and that model scale brings little benefit.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The authors analyzed a wide range of tasks and datasets to curate their benchmark
2. The authors conduct comprehensive experiments on multiple LLMs
3. The authors have in-depth discussions about reasoning models

limitations_weaknesses.value:
## Weakness
1. The naming of models in the paper is sometimes unclear or ambiguous, making it difficult for readers to understand or reproduce the experiments precisely. E.g. (1) Qwen2.5-32B should be notated as Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, as the former is also a model on Hugging Face. (2) The size of llama3.1 in Fig 3(a) and etc..
2. Fig 3 (b) and (c) show results of two types of models, which may indicate that the phenomenon found is not general for most LLMs.
3. The proposed LLM-as-a-Judge methods to detect abstention may not be accurate for reasoning models since the authors only tested and tuned the prompts on generations of two regular LLMs. Therefore such an evaluation metric may have bias on reasoning models.

## Questions and Suggestions:
1. Line 1052 “We use greedy decoding (i.e., temperature = 0) for judge inference”, this should be mentioned in the main paper.
2. I suggest the authors refer to OpenAI’s recent work on deliberative alignment to further discuss abstention and alignment perspectives in LLMs, especially for reasoning models.
3. In line 163, how many responses each LM will generate with a temperature of 0.8, and why use 0.8?
4. The authors can also conduct experiments on model size in Fig 3(b) for the Qwen series to derive a more general conclusion.

title.value: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions

TLDR.value: Our new benchmark AbstentionBench reveals reasoning models struggle to determine when not to answer.

abstract.value:
For Large Language Models (LLMs) to be reliably deployed in both everyday and high-stakes domains, knowing when not to answer is equally critical as answering correctly.
Real-world user queries, which can be underspecified, ill-posed, or fundamentally unanswerable, require LLMs to reason about uncertainty and selectively abstain---i.e., refuse to answer definitively.
However, abstention remains understudied, without a systematic evaluation framework for modern LLMs.
In this work, we introduce AbstentionBench: a large-scale benchmark for holistically evaluating abstention across 20 diverse datasets, including questions with unknown answers, underspecification, false premises, subjective interpretations, and outdated information.
Evaluating 20 frontier LLMs reveals abstention is an unsolved problem, and one where scaling models is of little use.
While recent reasoning LLMs have shown impressive results in complex problem solving, surprisingly, we find that reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention (by 24\% on average), even for math and science domains on which reasoning models are explicitly trained.
We find that while a carefully crafted system prompt can boost abstention in practice, it does not resolve models’ fundamental inability to reason about uncertainty.
We release AbstentionBench to foster research into advancing LLM reliability.

pdf.description: Upload your submission as a PDF file that ends with .pdf. In this file the main text (max. nine pages), references, and checklist may be followed by technical appendices, for which there is no page limit. Paper PDF can be updated until the full paper submission deadline (May 15).

dataset_submission.description: Indicate whether your submission includes a dataset. **If you check this box, you must provide a valid Croissant metadata file and a URL to your dataset accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** For detailed requirements, please refer to the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines).

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. If your submission has more than one Croissant metadata file, please package all files into a single ZIP archive and upload it here. **Before uploading, verify that your file is valid using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/JoaquinVanschoren/croissant-checker).** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_URL.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, provide the URL to your dataset here. **Before including the URL for your dataset, verify that you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines) (as part of the CFPs) and that the URL is accessible to NeurIPS2025 reviewers.** If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this field empty.

dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. See [https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/PaperChecklist) and the provided 2025 sample LaTeX file. **Papers not including the checklist in the paper PDF will be desk rejected.**

enum.description: I confirm that I have included a paper checklist in the paper PDF.

code_URL.description: If your submission includes code, provide the URL to a hosting platform (e.g., Github, Bitbucket) as described in the CFPs. See the main track [code guidelines](https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for details.

supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**

enum.description: We acknowledge the responsible reviewing obligations as authors.

primary_area.description: Please indicate the primary subject area that best describes the paper. This will be used for reviewer matching and submission statistics.

enum.description: Datasets & Benchmarks for applications in computer vision

Datasets & Benchmarks illustrating Different Deep learning Scenarios (e.g., architectures, generative models, optimization for deep networks, foundation models, LLMs)

Evaluation (e.g., data collection methodology, data processing methodology, data analysis methodology, meta studies on data sources, extracting signals from data, replicability of data collection and data analysis and validity of metrics, validity of data collection experiments, human-in-the-loop for data collection, human-in-the-loop for data evaluation)
Machine learning approaches to data and benchmarks enrichment, augmentation and processing (supervised, unsupervised, online, active, fine-tuning, RLHF, SFT, alignment, etc.)
AL/ML data processing and benchmarking Infrastructure (e.g., metrics libraries, visualization libraries, data exploration libraries, distributed data processing solutions, scalable data analysis)
AL/ML Datasets & Benchmarks for health sciences (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)
AL/ML Datasets & Benchmarks for life sciences (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)
AL/ML Datasets & Benchmarks for physics (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)
AL/ML Datasets & Benchmarks for social sciences (e.g. climate, health, life sciences, physics, social sciences)
Data and Benchmarking scenarios in Neuroscience and cognitive science (e.g., neural coding, brain-computer interfaces)
Dataset and Benchmark for Optimization (e.g., convex and non-convex, stochastic, robust, metrics for optimization, scaling of datasets, benchmarks)
Probabilistic methods  for dataset analysis and benchmarking (e.g., variational inference, causal inference, Gaussian processes)
Data for Reinforcement learning (e.g., decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics)
Social and economic aspects of datasets and benchmarks in machine learning (e.g., fairness, interpretability, human-AI interaction, privacy, safety, strategic behavior)
Other (please use sparingly, only use the keyword field for more details)

LLM_usage.description: This checklist collects statistical information on how NeurIPS authors use Generative AI (e.g., LLMs) in manuscript preparation. Responses are confidential and will not be shared with reviewers, area chairs, or senior chairs. The PC Chairs will analyze aggregated data to understand how emerging technologies influence the research publication process. Please select all that apply below.

items.description: Prefer not to declare (you can then skip the rest)
Not used at all (you can then skip the rest)
Editing (e.g., grammar, spelling, word choice)
Understanding technical concepts
Data processing/filtering
Visualizing results for submission
Facilitating or running experiments
Proving theorems
Implementing standard methods
Implementing methods where LLM plays an original, non-standard role
Other (enter in the text field below)
